title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
lead: Develop bubble, selection and insertion sorts while checking order, element preservation and the relative order of tied keys.
why: Sorting supports rankings, indexes and reports. Losing a record or silently rearranging tied events can be worse than a slow result. Algorithm selection therefore starts with a precise contract.
objectives: Trace insertion, selection and bubble with duplicate keys.
Choose an algorithm for a small nearly ordered collection.
prerequisites: Modules 1–3: validated input, functions, vector, records, references and lifetimes.
Direct learning dependencies: cpp.algorithm-complexity. New constructs are explained before the task.

concepts.definition: Preserving the original relative order of equivalent elements.
Adding the next item to a sorted prefix by shifting.
Finding the minimum of the suffix and placing it at the boundary.
Comparing neighbors and exchanging inverted pairs.
A property true before and after each iteration.
Moving an item to an adjacent position to make room.
Work that depends on order already present in the input.

sections.title: The complete sorting contract
paragraphs: For ascending integers, the result must be ordered and contain every original value with the same multiplicity. The second condition preserves the multiset. Replacing all items with zero can pass an order check but is not sorting. Records must retain their associated fields too: a key cannot be detached from its name or ID.

The lab automatically assigns each record an original position. key determines order while original makes rearrangements observable. n=0 is valid and prints an empty line. Reject out-of-range, missing or extra data before reporting a result; a partial output would otherwise resemble a successfully sorted collection.

sections.title: A comparison predicate defines the order
paragraphs: For our integers, a<b means “a should precede b”. Strictness requires that an item never precede itself. Transitivity connects three values: a<b and b<c imply a<c. Tied keys mean neither precedes the other. General library sorting requires a strict weak order, rather than an arbitrary function returning bool.

a<=b is not strict: tied values make it true in both directions. Do not pass it to a standard sort as an experiment; violating a library precondition is unsafe. Check the wrong rule separately as a relation on a small table. Shifting tied elements in insertion sort is a different, safely observable experiment about stability.

sections.title: Bubble: a finalized suffix
paragraphs: Scan left to right, swapping neighbors when the right key is smaller. After a pass, a maximum of the processed prefix is at its right end. The next pass can stop one position earlier because a suffix contains finalized maxima. The termination variant is the length of the unfinished region, which decreases after each pass.

Without early exit, neighbor comparisons total n(n−1)/2 even on sorted input. A changed flag can stop after a swap-free pass; reset it before each pass. Strict comparisons and adjacent swaps preserve tied-record order. For an empty vector, guard with end>1 instead of computing an unprotected size−1.

sections.title: Selection: minima on the left
paragraphs: At step i, find best, the position of a minimum key in [i,n), then swap records a[i] and a[best]. The invariant says positions before i contain their final smallest elements. The inner search does not mutate the array; the outer step finalizes one position. Trace best separately before doing the swap.

This version uses quadratic minimum-search comparisons in both best and worst cases. At most n−1 nontrivial swaps are needed, though the shown code also assigns when best==i. Ordinary selection sort is unstable: swapping first and last in (2,A),(2,B),(1,C) places B before A. Fewer swaps alone do not make it best for every record type.

sections.title: Insertion: a sorted prefix
paragraphs: Before step i, [0,i) is sorted. Copy a[i] into saved, then shift larger keys right until the insertion position is found. saved is necessary because shifting overwrites its original cell. After assigning a[j]=saved, [0,i+1) is sorted and contains the same multiset of records.

Test j>0 before reading a[j−1], protecting the left boundary. Stop shifting on equal keys so the new item stays after earlier ties; this gives stability. For sorted input with n≥1, there are n−1 key comparisons; reverse distinct input needs n(n−1)/2 shifts. Near-sortedness benefits insertion much more than selection.

sections.title: Stability and multiple keys
paragraphs: Stability does not make every input permutation produce the same result: tied keys retain that particular input order. If you need “score, then ID”, specify both keys. For equal-time events, retaining arrival order may be a domain requirement that an extra name sort would violate.

Distinguish the library promises used in the next lesson: ordinary sort does not guarantee stability, while stable_sort does. Neither removes comparator requirements. First trace labels A and B manually, then state what your ranking needs and which test distinguishes the implementations.

sections.title: Checking a sort independently
paragraphs: Check neighboring order, then length and value frequencies; for a stable version also check original order inside each tied-key group. Distinct-only data cannot test stability. Empty, singleton, equal, reverse, sorted and duplicate-containing inputs represent different classes, not decorative variations of one example.

For a small collection, independently write the expected result. Later we add a library oracle and property checks, but comparing two functions with the same defect is not independence. Input permutation and sorting twice provide useful extra checks. They strengthen tests without replacing invariants and boundary reasoning.

sections.title: Choosing an implementation and the task boundary
paragraphs: Manual sorts here teach state, invariants and cost. Normal development should first consider an appropriate library algorithm. Selection depends on size, data structure, comparison/move cost and stability requirements. Success on 32 items is not evidence for the fastest algorithm on large logs.

Submit stable insertion source, a one-pass trace, expected and actual cases, and a worst-case shift argument. As an extension, add bubble’s early exit without changing its contract. The next lesson separates a container from traversal through iterators and introduces standard algorithms as composable tools.

steps: After a pass the active-prefix maximum is on the right.
